summary: A fictional first-person narrator walks with a mysterious, persuasive man along bluffs overlooking the Hudson River. He explains the ancient Greek healing schools of Asklepios (drugs from outside the body) and Hygeia (healing from within by governing one's own body). He then links the Hygeian approach to infertility, claiming a childless woman's body is out of harmony and that he restores it with Eastern practices and herbal therapies. The narrator, whose Western medicine has failed, grows interested but remains wary of him.
one_line: A narrator on Hudson River bluffs hears a smooth healer contrast Asklepios's drug-based medicine with Hygeia's self-healing school and claim it can treat infertility.
key_facts: The narrator and a man walk along a cobblestone path leading west to a line of bluffs overlooking the Hudson.
The early spring wind was cutting into the narrator's face, causing the nostrils to feel on fire.
The man describes Asklepios as the ancient Greek god of medicine.
The physicians who revered Asklepios held that sickness could be cured using drugs and potions that came from outside the body.
The man says billion-dollar industries thrive by enhancing the arsenal of antibiotics.
Hygeia is named as the daughter of Asklepios and the goddess of health.
The Hygeians believed wellness originated from properly governing one's own body.
The Hygeian ideal was healing from within rather than intervention from without.
The man says the Hygeian school more or less died out in the West but lives on in other places.
He claims primitive peoples use natural herbs to enhance their own immune system rather than manufactured, synthetic drugs.
The man states that if a woman is childless, the reason is more often than not that her body is out of harmony with itself.
He says he seeks out each woman's unique energy flows and attempts to restore them using Eastern practices and Hygeian herbal therapies.
He admits that some women's bodies are naturally unresponsive, and in those cases he tries to provide a child by other means.
When asked, he replies 'By whatever means seems appropriate,' cryptically, and the narrator suggests adoption.
The narrator says Western medicine had completely struck out for them and that the man was a little too smooth.
